newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms' copper sales fall on S'tomo scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms' copper sales fall on S'tomo scandal.

text.p: Major Japanese trading firms said on Tuesday their sales of refined copper in the half year to September fell steadily in the wake of the Sumitomo scandal and the metal's price plunges.

But Sumitomo Corp, which announced earlier this year losses of $2.6 billion which it blamed on unauthorised copper deals by its former chief trader, still remained the top merchant of the red metal in Japan.

Sumitomo said its refined copper sales in the period, the first half of the 1996/97 business year, plunged to 181.2 billion yen ($1.61 billion), down 243.3 billion yen ($2.17 billion) or 57 percent from the same period the previous year, in the wake of the scandal.
Before trader Yasuo Hamanaka was fired by Sumitomo in mid-June, he was widely regarded as the most influential and controversial player in the world copper market.
Sumitomo has accused Hamanaka of racking up estimated losses of $2.6 billion from unauthorised copper trading in what has been called the biggest-ever loss on financial markets.
"Since Hamanaka was fired in June we've being handling only necessary copper business, such as long-term contracts," said Sumitomo executive vice president Takehiko Yonezu.
Hamanaka was arrested on suspicion of forgery on October 22 in connection with the trades, and also faces fraud charges.

Mitsui & Co Ltd said its copper sales fell to 155.4 billion yen ($1.38 billion) in the April-September period from 186.5 billion yen ($1.66 billion) a year earlier, as the metal price plunged after the Sumitomo scandal.
The scandal precipitated a tumble in world copper prices in May and June of more than one-third, to their lowest levels in 2-1/2 years.
"The price plunges earlier must have erased part of the profit margins and sales," Yoshiaki Oonuki, managing director of Mitsui & Co Ltd, told reporters. ($1=112 yen)
